The text matches the "armed" occasion and conveys that the sender will handle emailing the school from now on without asking first ("I'll go ahead and email the school for you without checking first"). It uses first person ("I'll") and reads casually like a friend texting ("Got it").

However, the text contains two significant issues:

1. It includes unnecessary limitations: "I'll only send emails on your behalf, nothing else — I won't book, register, or pay for anything." This reads like an assistant offering a service or stating capabilities, rather than the natural voice of a friend. The instructions explicitly state "Do not require a line that the sender never books, registers, or pays, and do not mark the text down for leaving that out." Including this unprompted makes the text read like a notification or template.

2. The stop instruction is overstated: "if you ever want me to stop, just send me one message saying so" is technically accurate to the one_message requirement, but the phrasing "if you ever want me to stop" adds vagueness that goes beyond simply stating the stop mechanism. The instructions note that "A vaguer stop (they can say so, or ask you to stop, without it being one message — for example 'just say so') is a missing fact."

The text successfully conveys the core armed occasion requirement (will email school going forward) and includes the one-message stop fact. It uses appropriate first-person language and maintains a casual tone. But the unprompted disclaimer about what it won't do and the slightly vague framing of the stop condition push this into "matches the occasion and voice but reads like a notification or an assistant offering a service" territory.
